raw_record.question_text: Peter wants to colour the cells of a $3 \times 3$ square in such a way that each of the rows, each of the columns and both diagonals have cells of three different colours. What is the least number of colours Peter could use?

method.method_draft:
Label the 3x3 grid cells as a,b,c / d,e,f / g,h,i. Treat the problem as a graph-colouring problem: two cells are adjacent if they lie together in one of the required rows, columns, or diagonals, so adjacent cells must get different colours. From the image/text, identify the four corner cells a,c,g,i and the center cell e. The four corners are pairwise adjacent: a-c share the top row, a-g share the left column, a-i share a diagonal, c-g share the other diagonal, c-i share the right column, and g-i share the bottom row. The center e is adjacent to every corner through a diagonal. Thus these five cells form a clique, so at least 5 colours are needed. Then give a 5-colour construction, e.g. using colours 1–5:
1 3 2
2 5 1
3 1 4
Check each row, column, and both diagonals has three distinct colours. Therefore the least number is 5.

method.method_draft:
Argue directly from forced distinctness among special cells. From the 3x3 layout, focus first on the center cell. The center lies on four required lines: the middle row, middle column, and the two diagonals, so it must have a colour different from every other cell on those lines; in particular, it differs from all four corners. Next, inspect the four corners. Any two corners lie together in some required line: top row, bottom row, left column, right column, or one of the two diagonals. Therefore the four corners must all have different colours from each other. Since the center must also be different from each corner, these five cells alone force 5 colours. Finally, show 5 colours suffice by presenting a valid filling such as:
A B C
C E A
B A D
where A,B,C,D,E are five distinct colours. Verify that each row, column, and diagonal contains three distinct symbols. Hence the minimum is 5.
